meaning: Links two sentences or two items. It shows the order of actions, or adds one more point to what came before.
connection: Sentence. そして、sentence / Noun、そして noun

senses.label: Sequence: and then
senses.meaning: Actions happen one after another in time, like “and then” or “next”. Usually the same person does both actions. It sounds a little more formal than 「それから」.
senses.connection: Action sentence. そして、action sentence (often with 「まず」 and 「最後に」)
examples: I ate breakfast. And then I went to school.
First, wash your hands. Then cook the food.

senses.label: Adding: and also
senses.meaning: Adds one more item to what you just said, like “and also” or “what's more”. Often used to list features of a person or thing.
senses.connection: Adjective / noun sentence. そして、adjective / noun sentence
examples: This room is spacious. And it's very bright, too.
I can speak Japanese, English, and Chinese.

senses.label: Result: and so
senses.meaning: Something develops from what came before and leads to a result, like “and so” or “in the end”. Common in stories and written texts.
senses.connection: Narrative sentence. そして、result sentence (usually in the た-form)
examples: He practiced every day. And he won the match.
The two of them met. And then they got married.

notes: 「そして」 only continues in the same direction. It can't introduce something contrary or unexpected: ✕「雨が降りました。そして、試合はありました。」→ ○「雨が降りました。でも、試合はありました。」
To join two nouns, normally use 「と」 or 「や」: ✕「パンそして牛乳を買いました」→ ○「パンと牛乳を買いました」. 「AとB、そしてC」 is used only when you reach the last item of a list and want to highlight it.

Starting every sentence with 「そして」 sounds like a child's school essay. For one person's actions in a row, the te-form inside a single sentence is more natural: ✕「起きました。そして、食べました。そして、出かけました。」→ ○「起きて、朝ご飯を食べてから、出かけました。」
To nudge someone on with “And then?” while listening, say 「それで？」 or 「それから？」, not ✕「そして？」.
To state a clear cause-and-effect “so”, use 「それで」 or 「だから」. 「そして」 simply tells what came next and doesn't stress a reason.

daily.title: Talking about your day
daily.description: Telling a friend, or writing in a diary, what you did in order.
daily.example: Yesterday I went shopping. And then I saw a movie.

daily.title: Introducing yourself
daily.example: I'm a student. I also work part-time at a café.

daily.title: Reading a fairy tale
daily.description: Fairy tales and picture books often use 「そして」 to move the story forward.
daily.example: And they lived happily ever after.

work.title: Explaining steps
work.description: Walking a coworker or client through how to do something.
work.example: Press this button. Then please enter your name.

work.title: Wrapping up a talk
work.description: Listing key points in a speech and adding one last item.
work.example: Quality, price, and service are all important.

etymology: Generally thought to be a shortened form of 「そうして」: the adverb 「そう」 (that way) plus 「して」, the te-form of 「する」. It first meant “having done so”, and later became fixed as a conjunction.
formation: 「そして」 = the demonstrative adverb 「そう」 (“that way”) + 「して」, the te-form of 「する」: it is a contraction of 「そうして」. 「そう」 points back to the whole content of the previous sentence, and 「して」 uses the te-form's “sequence / linking” function to connect it to the next thing. Literally, it means “having done it that way”. Because its core is the te-form, it can show the order of actions (“and then”) as well as listing and adding (“and also”). After a chain of events, “carrying on like that” naturally leads to a final outcome, which gives the “and so, in the end” use. The te-form itself only links things in the same direction and has no contrastive element, so 「そして」 can't be followed by something that goes against the previous sentence.

similar.title: 〜それから (at the start: after that / also)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can mean “and then”. 「それから」 stresses the time order “after that”, and in speech it often adds a new topic (“also”). 「そして」 is better for adding points and stating results, and sounds slightly more written.

similar.title: 〜て (te-form: linking and sequence)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can show the order of actions. The te-form links actions inside one sentence (「食べて、出かけた」); 「そして」 starts a new sentence and joins two independent sentences, with a stronger pause.

similar.title: 〜それに (at the start: besides / on top of that)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can add “what's more”. 「それに」 is mostly spoken and adds one more reason to a list (「安いし、それに近い」). 「そして」 just adds smoothly, without the “and on top of that” tone.

similar.title: 〜それで (at the start: so / that's why)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can lead into “what happened next”. 「それで」 clearly marks the previous sentence as the cause (“so”); 「そして」 only says one thing followed another, with no clear causal link.

meaning: Shows time order (“after that”). It is also used to add something (“also”, “and”).
connection: Sentence. それから、sentence / Noun、それから noun

senses.label: Time: after that
senses.meaning: You do one thing after finishing another, like “then” or “after that”. The focus is on the order in time.
senses.connection: Action sentence. それから、action sentence
examples: I got up at seven. Then I took a shower.
I walk to the station, and then take a bus.

senses.label: Adding: also
senses.meaning: Adds another item to what you've already said, like “also” or “and”. Common when ordering food or listing things.
senses.connection: Noun / sentence. それから、what you add
examples: Two coffees, and one piece of cake, please.
Also, please come at eight tomorrow.

senses.label: Ever since then
senses.meaning: A state that has continued from a certain point in time, like “since then”. Usually followed by something ongoing.
senses.connection: Talking about the past. それから(は)、ongoing state
examples: I came to Japan last year. Since then, I've been living in Tokyo.

notes: 「それから」 goes at the start of a sentence, and a complete sentence must come before it. It can't attach directly to a verb: ✕「ご飯を食べたそれから、出かけます」→ ○「ご飯を食べてから、出かけます」 or 「ご飯を食べます。それから、出かけます」.
A bare 「それから？」 (“And then?”) is very casual. Said to a boss or a client, it can sound like an interrogation. Use a full polite question instead, such as 「それから、どうなりましたか」.
In reports and formal writing, adding point after point with 「それから」 sounds conversational. In writing, 「また」 or 「さらに」 is usually used to add items.

When 「それ」 refers to a concrete thing, 「それから」 just means literally “from that”: 「それから一つ選んでください」 is “Please choose one of those”, not “Then choose one”. Check whether 「それ」 can point to something mentioned earlier.

daily.title: Ordering food
daily.description: Ordering dishes one by one at a restaurant.
daily.example: One ramen. And a beer too, please.

daily.title: Listening to a friend's story
daily.description: Urging a friend to go on with a story.

daily.title: Weekend plans
daily.description: Telling your family what you'll do, in order.
daily.example: On Saturday I'm going to the library. After that, I'm meeting a friend.

work.title: Adding an item at a meeting
work.description: Adding one more announcement before a meeting ends.
work.example: Also, next week's meeting will be on the third floor.

work.title: Explaining the order of tasks
work.description: A senior coworker explains the order of work to a newcomer.
work.example: First check your email, and then please make the documents.

etymology: Made from the pronoun 「それ」 (that) and the particle 「から」 (from), literally “from that (point in time)”. It grew into a conjunction meaning “after that” and “also”.
formation: 「それから」 = the demonstrative 「それ」 (“that”: what was just said, or that point in time) + the case particle 「から」, which marks a starting point (“from”). Literally, “from that”. Counting forward from the previous event gives time order: “then, after that”. Continuing on from that point gives “ever since then”. In conversation, taking what has already been said as the starting point and carrying on gives the topic-adding “also, and another thing”. Because its core is a starting point, it always implies that the previous event or remark is finished first, so its sense of time order is stronger than that of 「そして」.

similar.title: 〜そして (at the start: and then / and also)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can mean “and then”. 「そして」 focuses on continuing and adding, and can also lead into a result; 「それから」 focuses on time order (“after that”) and adding topics, and is more common in speech.

similar.title: 〜てから
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “first A, then B”. 「〜てから」 links inside one sentence and stresses that B happens only after A is done; 「それから」 comes at the start of a sentence and joins two sentences.

similar.title: 〜それに (at the start: besides / on top of that)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can add something. With 「それから」 the addition is just “one more thing”, typical when ordering food or passing on tasks; 「それに」 adds one more reason or opinion, with a building “and what's more” tone.

similar.title: 〜から (starting point)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「から」 in 「それから」 is the 「から」 that marks a starting point. 「駅から歩く」 is a starting point in space; 「それから」 takes the previous event as a starting point in time, and has become a fixed conjunction.

meaning: The particle 「と」 has several uses: it quotes what is said or thought (〜と言う・〜と思う), links nouns to mean “and” or marks a partner in a joint or mutual action, and expresses a condition meaning “whenever / as soon as ...”.
connection: 「Exact words」 / plain-form sentence (noun / na-adjective + だ) + と + 言う・思う・聞く; noun + と + noun / verb; verb dictionary form / ない form + と (condition)

senses.label: Quotation (direct and indirect)
senses.meaning: Reports what someone said. A direct quotation keeps the exact words inside 「」; an indirect quotation turns the content into a plain-form sentence, and 「だ」 is often added after nouns and na-adjectives.
senses.connection: 「Exact words」 / plain-form sentence (noun / na-adjective + だ) + と + 言う／言っていた
examples: The teacher said, “There's a test tomorrow.”
Mr. Tanaka said he isn't coming tomorrow.
My mother says she likes this shop.

senses.label: Thoughts and opinions
senses.meaning: 「と思う」 gives the speaker's thought or judgment, like “I think”. It sounds softer than stating something flatly.
senses.connection: Plain-form sentence (noun / na-adjective + だ) + と + 思う／思います
examples: I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think this movie is interesting.
I think he's a student.

senses.label: Hearing, writing, and more
senses.meaning: 「と」 also goes with 「聞く」, 「書く」, 「答える」, 「呼ぶ」 and similar verbs, to give what was heard, written, answered, or what something is called.
senses.connection: Content + と + 聞く・書く・答える・呼ぶ・伝える
examples: I heard on the news that a typhoon is coming.
I wrote “thank you” in the letter.
He answered, “Yes.”

senses.label: Listing (and)
senses.meaning: Lists nouns one by one: “A and B”. 「と」 gives a complete list: these items and nothing else. It can only join nouns, not verbs or adjectives.
senses.connection: Noun + と + noun (+ と + noun)
examples: I bought bread and milk.
There are a book and a pen on the desk.
My family is my father, my mother and my younger sister.

senses.label: Doing something together
senses.meaning: Shows who you do something with: “with”. 「〜と一緒に」 (“together with”) is also common and makes the meaning clearer.
senses.connection: Person + と (一緒に) + verb
examples: Yesterday I saw a movie with a friend.
This weekend I'm traveling with my family.
I went shopping with my mother.

senses.label: Partner in a mutual action
senses.meaning: Marks the other person in an action that needs two sides: “marry”, “argue with”, “talk with”. These verbs can't take 「一緒に」.
senses.connection: Person + と + 結婚する／話す／会う／けんかする／相談する
examples: I'm getting married to my girlfriend next year.
Yesterday I talked with my teacher.
I had a fight with my younger brother.

senses.label: Natural result
senses.meaning: Once A happens, B always follows. Used for natural laws, operating machines, giving directions, etc. Like “when / whenever ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / nai-form + と (〜になると・〜を押すと・まっすぐ行くと)
examples: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
If you press this button, water comes out.
My dad turns on the TV as soon as he gets home.

senses.label: Discovery
senses.meaning: 「〜と、〜た」 means that after doing A, you found B. The second clause is in the past and is often something unexpected.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + と、〜た (窓を開けると、〜ていた)
examples: When I opened the window, it was snowing.
When I got home, my mother was there.

notes: In indirect quotes, add 「だ」 after nouns and na-adjectives: ✕「学生と思う」→ ○「学生だと思う」; ✕「静かと言った」→ ○「静かだと言った」.

Quotative 「と」 follows a sentence, while 「と」 meaning “with” follows a person or thing. Mixing them up changes the meaning completely: 「友達と言いました」 is “I said it together with a friend”, but 「友達だと言いました」 is “(he) said (they) were a friend”.
「と」 gives a complete list; to give just a few examples, use 「や」: 「パンと牛乳を買った」 (bought only these two things); 「パンや牛乳を買った」 (bought these and other things).
The partner in mutual actions like 「結婚する」 or 「けんかする」 takes 「と」, not 「を」: ✕「彼女を結婚します」→ ○「彼女と結婚します」.
The second clause can't be an intention, wish, command, or request: ✕「駅に着くと、電話してください」→ ○「駅に着いたら、電話してください」; ✕「お金があると、旅行したい」→ ○「お金があったら、旅行したい」.

daily.title: Passing on a family member's words
daily.description: Telling a friend what someone in your family said.
daily.example: My older sister said she was going to bed.

daily.title: Sharing your impressions
daily.description: Giving your opinion after a movie.
daily.example: I think the last scene was good.

daily.title: Weekend chat
daily.description: Friends talking about who they went out with.
daily.example: On Sunday I went shopping with my older sister.

daily.title: At a convenience store
daily.description: Telling the clerk what you want.
daily.example: A rice ball and a tea, please.

daily.title: Giving directions
daily.description: A local explains the way to a tourist.
daily.example: Turn right at the second corner, and you'll see the station.

work.title: Giving your opinion at a meeting
work.description: Using 「と思います」 to state your view politely.
work.example: I think this plan is good.

work.title: Passing on a phone message
work.description: Telling your boss what a client said on the phone.
work.example: Mr. Yamada called to say he'll be a little late for the meeting.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Telling your boss you discussed something with a client.
work.example: I talked it over with the client yesterday.

work.title: Instruction manual
work.description: A manual describes what happens when you operate a device.
work.example: When you turn on the power, the lamp lights up.

etymology: 「と」 is a case particle already found in Old Japanese. Its core idea is “pairing two things as a set”: it pairs nouns (and, together with), pairs a content with the act of saying or thinking (quotation), and later developed into a conjunctive particle that pairs two clauses (condition).
formation: All the senses come from the same idea of tightly pairing what comes before と with what comes after. Noun + と + noun pairs two things (“and”); person + と + verb pairs that person as a partner in the action (together, mutual actions); content + と + 言う・思う pairs the content with the act of saying or thinking, like putting quotation marks around it (quotation); clause + と + clause pairs two events so that B follows automatically once A occurs (condition). To tell them apart, look at what is around 「と」: between nouns it usually means “and”, after a full sentence followed by 言う・思う it is a quotation, and before another clause expressing a natural result it is a condition.

similar.title: 〜って (quotation, topic)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「って」 is the casual spoken form of quotative 「と」, common between friends (「明日休みだって」). In formal situations and in writing, use 「と」.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: Both list things with “and” and are close in meaning: 「と」 gives a complete list (only these); 「や」 gives a partial list (a few examples, there are others).

similar.title: 〜ば (hypothetical)
similar.explanation: Both are conditionals. 「ば」 focuses on the condition itself (“as long as ..., then ...”), and when both clauses share a subject, the second can be an intention or wish (「時間があれば、行きたい」). 「と」 focuses on an inevitable result, and its second clause can't be volitional.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「たら」 has the widest range, and its second clause can be a request or intention (「着いたら電話して」). 「と」 is limited to natural laws, operating machines, habits, and “discoveries”. In everyday conversation, 「たら」 is the safest choice when unsure.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「なら」 picks up the other person's topic and gives advice (「京都へ行くなら、新幹線がいい」), with no time sequence between the clauses. 「と」 means the second event follows as soon as the first one happens.

meaning: Use “noun + の + position word” to say where something is: on the desk, in front of the station, inside the box.
connection: Noun + の + 前・上・中・下・横・隣 etc. + に／で／を

senses.label: Above, below, inside, outside
senses.meaning: Gives a position relative to something: on, under, inside, outside. 「の」 is required: 「机の上」 (on the desk), literally “the desk's top”.
senses.connection: Noun + の + 上・下・中・外 + に (existence) ／ で (action)
examples: There's a book on the desk.
My wallet is in the bag.
There's a cat under the bed.

senses.label: Front, back, left, right
senses.meaning: Gives directions such as in front, behind, left, right, and beside. 「横」 is simply “beside”; 「隣」 means “next door” or right next to something of the same kind.
senses.connection: Noun + の + 前・後ろ・右・左・横・隣・そば
examples: I'm waiting in front of the station.
There's a convenience store next to the bank.
Please stand behind Mr. Tanaka.

senses.label: Between and near
senses.meaning: 「間」 means “between two things”, usually as 「AとBの間」. 「近く」 and 「そば」 mean “near”.
senses.connection: AとB + の + 間 ／ Noun + の + 近く・そば
examples: There's a park between the post office and the hospital.
There's a supermarket near my house.

notes: English says “in the bag” or “on the desk” with a preposition, but in Japanese the 「の」 can't be dropped: ✕「かばん中に財布があります」→ ○「かばんの中に財布があります」.
Use 「に」 for where something is, and 「で」 for where an action happens. Mixing them up is the most common mistake: ✕「公園の中に遊びます」→ ○「公園の中で遊びます」; ✕「机の上で本があります」→ ○「机の上に本があります」.
For “behind” in space, use 「後ろ」. 「の後（あと）」 means “after” in time: ✕「駅の後に公園があります」→ ○「駅の後ろに公園があります」; 「食事の後」 means “after the meal”.
「の前」 can mean either place or time: 「駅の前で待つ」 (in front of the station) / 「食事の前に手を洗う」 (before the meal). Whether the word before it is a place or an event decides whether it's about space or time.

daily.title: Looking for something
daily.description: A family member asks where the keys are.
daily.example: The keys are on the table.

daily.title: Choosing a meeting place
daily.description: Deciding with a friend where to meet.
daily.example: OK, let's meet in front of the station.

daily.title: Giving directions
daily.description: Telling someone on the street where a place is.
daily.example: The library is on the other side of the park.

work.title: Explaining where a room is
work.description: Telling a visitor where the meeting room is.
work.example: The meeting room is to the right of the elevator.

work.title: Finding documents
work.description: Telling a coworker where you put some documents.
work.example: The documents are in the drawer of my desk.

etymology: Position words like 「前」, 「上」, and 「中」 are nouns themselves. So, like any noun, they are described with “noun + の”. Literally, it's “the desk's top” or “the station's front”.
formation: Position words like 「前・上・中・下」 are independent nouns in Japanese, not prepositions. So “on the desk” has to be said as “the desk's | top” = 「机の上」: the noun-linking 「の」 connects the reference object to the position noun. Once linked, 「机の上」 as a whole is a place noun, and you add whatever particle you need: 「に」 for where something is, 「で」 for where an action happens, 「を」 for a place you pass through. “Reference + の + position noun” only sets a relative position: when the reference is an object, it's about space; when it's an event, it's about time. That's why 「駅の前」 is in front of the station and 「食事の前」 is before the meal.

similar.title: 〜まえに
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「前」. 「〜の前」 in this entry mainly shows a position in space, “in front of”; 「〜まえに」 shows time, “before”. It attaches directly to the dictionary form of a verb (「寝る前に」), while nouns need 「の」 (「食事の前に」).

similar.title: 〜間・〜間に
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「間」. 「AとBの間」 in this entry is “between” in space; 「〜間・〜間に」 means “during” in time, as in 「夏休みの間」.

similar.title: 〜の中で〜がいちばん
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「の中」. 「の中」 in this entry is “inside” in space (「箱の中」); 「〜の中で一番」 compares things within a group: “the most … among …”.

similar.title: 〜中（じゅう・ちゅう）
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「中」. 「の中（なか）」 in this entry is the inside of something; 「〜中（じゅう）」 after a noun means “all over / throughout” (「世界中」「一日中」), and 「〜中（ちゅう）」 means “in the middle of” (「会議中」).

meaning: In everyday conversation, particles like 「は」, 「を」, 「が」, and 「へ・に」 are often dropped. This makes speech sound casual and friendly.
connection: Noun (は・を・が・へ dropped) + predicate (mostly casual, plain form)

senses.label: Dropping 「は」
senses.meaning: The 「は」 after a topic is often dropped and replaced by a pause or comma. Common when introducing yourself or pointing at something. It sounds relaxed and natural.
senses.connection: 私・これ・それ etc. + (は)、 + predicate
examples: I'm Tanaka.
This is good, isn't it?

senses.label: Dropping 「を」
senses.meaning: The 「を」 after an object is very often dropped in speech, especially in everyday questions like 「ご飯食べた？」.
senses.connection: Noun + (を) + 食べる・飲む・見る・する etc.
examples: Have you eaten?
Want some tea?
Did you do your homework?

senses.label: Dropping 「が」
senses.meaning: The 「が」 for existence, states, and natural events is also often dropped, as in “I'm hungry” or “I have no time”.
senses.connection: Noun + (が) + ある・ない・すく・降る etc.
examples: I'm hungry.
I don't have time today.

senses.label: Dropping 「へ・に」
senses.meaning: The 「へ」 or 「に」 for a destination is also often dropped in speech before 「行く」, 「来る」, or 「帰る」.
senses.connection: Place noun + (へ・に) + 行く・来る・帰る
examples: Are you going to school tomorrow?
Where are you going?

notes: Dropping particles only suits casual talk with friends and family. When speaking to a boss or client, and in written texts or exam essays, use all the particles. Otherwise you'll sound casual and careless, and in an essay it will be marked wrong.

Only 「は・を・が・へ」, whose meaning is obvious, can be dropped. 「と・で・から・まで」 carry specific meanings, and dropping them changes the sentence: ✕「友達行く」 sounds like “my friend goes” → ○「友達と行く」 (I'll go with a friend).
The emphatic 「が」 meaning “this very person” can't be dropped. When asked 「誰が行く？」, answer 「私が行きます」; saying 「私行きます」 loses the “I'm the one going” emphasis.
When you drop 「は」, pause briefly after the topic (a comma in writing): 「私、田中です」. Said without a pause, it sounds like one word and is hard to follow.

daily.title: Questions at home
daily.description: A mother asks her child whether they've eaten.

daily.title: Inviting a friend out
daily.description: Casually asking a friend if they want to go somewhere.
daily.example: Want to go see a movie this weekend?

daily.title: Watching Japanese dramas and anime
daily.description: Dialogue on screen often drops particles, so fill in the meaning as you listen.

work.title: Chatting with a close coworker
work.description: Talking casually with a coworker you know well at lunch.

etymology: In Japanese, word order and context are often enough to show how the parts of a sentence relate. So in speech, obvious particles tend to be dropped. This is generally seen as a natural feature of speech aiming for brevity and closeness, not a grammar mistake.
formation: This entry isn't a specific grammar word, but the habit of leaving the particle out of “noun + (particle) + predicate”. Japanese uses particles to show how the parts of a sentence relate, but in face-to-face conversation, context, word order and the verb itself often already show who does what to what. In 「ご飯食べた？」, the rice can only be what gets eaten, so leaving out 「を」 causes no confusion. That's why the droppable particles are the most “empty” ones, the easiest to guess from the verb: 「は・を・が・へ」. 「と・で・から・まで」 express concrete meanings such as “together with”, place, starting point and end point; without them, nothing can be guessed, so they can't be dropped. Dropping particles makes sentences shorter and closer to how people who know each other talk, which is why it has a casual, friendly tone.

similar.title: 〜は (topic)
similar.explanation: The full form with the same meaning: 「私、田中です」 = 「私は田中です」. In writing and polite situations, write 「は」; in speech it's often dropped and replaced by a pause.

similar.title: 〜を (object)
similar.explanation: The full form with the same meaning: 「ご飯食べた？」 = 「ご飯を食べた？」. 「を」 is the particle most often dropped in speech, but it must be written in formal texts.

similar.title: 〜が (subject)
similar.explanation: The full form with the same meaning: 「お腹すいた」 = 「お腹がすいた」. 「が」 for existence or something happening can often be dropped, but 「が」 that stresses “this very one” can't.

similar.title: 〜って (quotation, topic)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: in speech, 「って」 often replaces 「は」 to bring up a topic (「田中さんって、どんな人？」). This isn't dropping a particle but switching to a casual one, with a “speaking of…” tone.
